summary: All three Shorts stalled at the new-channel test ceiling: 653, 1,150 and 1,168 views in their first wave, 0 shares, 1 subscriber, and 97–98 % of views from the Shorts feed. Only Yellow Fleet got a second push (+1,144 views between 23.10 and 25.10). The topics are not what failed. The failures are in execution and can be timed to the second. One method note first: the API retention curve and AVP count only viewers who did not swipe. Mean audienceWatchRatio equals AVP (0.540/0.468/0.851 vs 53/45/81 %), and minutes×60 divided by engaged views equals AVD. So Yellow Fleet's "81 %" means 81 % of the 40 % who stayed. Per 100 feed views, only 15 (Volcano), 9 (Rabbits) and 18.5 (Yellow Fleet) plays are still running at the last second. Volcano lost 34 % of its non-swipers in 5.4–10 s, exactly on the meta line plus "1935, Hawaii." over a globe dive and a satellite map. Its relative retention hit 0.255 there, the bottom quarter of similar-length videos. Rabbits lost 60 % in 5–19.5 s while it walked through an Australia map, "≈600 million by 1950 (CSIRO)", a £25,000 prize card, Pasteur and the Rodd Island lab (relative 0.242). Both then gave up another 40–48 % of their remaining viewers on a static scoreboard outro after the payoff. Yellow Fleet is the opposite case. Its body and loop are the best on the channel (AVP 81 %, relative retention 0.83 at the end, replay proxy 0.43 vs 0.20), but its first 5 s are a near-still canal with a title card and no living being (motion 0.56–0.87). 60 % of feed viewers swiped it. Measured against the reference medians, all three are slower than even the flop group: 0 hard cuts (dissolve-only style rule) vs 2.0 for flops, motion in second 0–1 of 4.0/1.9/0.7 vs 10.3, and 1.9–2.7 words/s vs 2.9. Rabbits had the best stayed rate (61 %) because the story's own animals were acting at frame 0 under a riddle line. That suggests "subject doing the absurd thing at frame 0" matters more than the mascot (hypothesis, N=3).

summary: Pig War, AI farm girl and Conman Russell all fail the same way. The story is clear, and viewers who get past the first seconds mostly stay. The problems are in the first 0–7 s and in the editing. Pig War is the only one of the three with an Analytics curve. Its first ~3 s are a map with no living being (motion 1.08; viral median 23.6). The premise is fully told by 3.9 s ("over one pig"). Then the backstory starts ("A farmer caught it…" with a "Lyman Cutlar, June 1859" label). Seconds 4–7 alone account for 27.8 % of the curve's total decline (a 7.5× faster loss than the body), and the end question "Team farmer or team pig?" loses another 14 %. Its body is exactly YouTube-median (relativeRetentionPerformance mean 0.50), and it had 0 shares. Views went ~80/h in the first hours, then ~4.7/h. The final 1,408 is the same as the 30+ other Pig War Shorts (0.1–2.4K). AI farm girl is the channel's worst: 130 views at 33 h, 39.5 % stayed (Studio), likes 1.5 %. Yet it has the best words/s (3.31) and decent pixel motion (13.5). So the meters can be fooled: the motion comes from overlaid SOLD stamps over a still, calm man. Nothing strange is said or shown until 14.9 s, and the twist at 20.3 s comes at about the average watch time (20 s). Across 5 Shorts, motion in the first second does not predict stayed (Spearman −0.10). Conman is the best of the three: a living being acting at frame 0, motion 19.6 in 0–1 s and 10.6 in 1–6 s, "four times" said by 3.0 s, a seamless loop and 115 views/h at 10 h. That is the channel's normal good pace (Yellow Fleet 124/h), not viral. It has no retention data yet, and the same Russell story already has 8 recent Shorts at a median of 1,242 views. All three use soft transitions with almost no hard cuts (0.73–0.92 per 10 s vs viral 3.6, flops 2.0). Verdict: the topics can reach 1M (each has one big hit), but our execution is median, so we get the median result for the 30th copy of a topic. Everything with N=1–5 below is marked as a hypothesis.

summary: The channel is flat, not rising. Views in the first ~10 h went 53 > 286 > 1,101 > 788 > <85 > 1,174, so it ramped over uploads 1-3 and then stopped at about 1.1K per Short. No Short has passed 2,312. In a sample of 188 brand-new niche channels, the 75th-percentile views stay at ~1.2-1.4K for every upload from #1 to #10. That looks like the default first test YouTube gives a new channel, and ATLAS APE reached it at upload #3 and has stayed there. ATLAS APE does better than most newcomers (78th-87th percentile), but only ~10 % of new channels get a single Short to 10K in their first 6 uploads (8.4 % in English), and ~1 in 80 gets a 1M in its first 10. Among 35 channels that looked like us after 6 Shorts, only 2 passed 10K in uploads 7-10. More uploads of the same thing is not the way out. The hook metric (Studio stayed %) has not improved: 57.6, 62.6, 42.8, 54.1, 39.5 %. In Isaac's benchmark, ~60 % stayed gave ~1.1K views at 24 h and 79.6 % gave 21K. Shortening clearly helped the body (AVP 53 to 81 %, end retention 15 to 47 %), and views of the 4 Shorts with Analytics rank by AVP and shortness. Only Yellow Fleet got a real second wave (+1,144 after day 2); Pig War's later views were the tail of its first wave. Farm girl was held back from the start (85 at 18 h vs ~1K for others with similar stayed %), so the owner should check Studio for a copyright claim on the meme clips. The big execution change in #5 and #6 (motion 0-1 s 13-20, 3.1-3.3 words/s) has not produced a better result yet: farm girl is the worst, and Russell is stuck on the same 1,174 first test. Viewers who watch like it at least as much as the owner's German channel (likes/1k 15.4 vs 11.7), but there are 0 shares and very few comments. That German channel's first 6 Shorts got 20-88K each (median 67K, 57 times ours) with 52-74 s videos, so the gap is distribution (market plus one fixed topic and format), not production quality. Packaging touches only ~3 % of current views (97 % come from the Shorts feed), so it cannot explain the plateau. Still, the channel page is broken: empty description, a GEOGRAPHY · MAPS · FACTS banner on a channel of absurd true stories, no playlists, four spellings of the name, and Atlas fading out of the videos. All 4 kit titles were changed at upload, with every emoji dropped. Missing data: N=6, Analytics only through PT 22.10, and Russell is only 10 h old, so every causal read is a hypothesis.

summary: The niche is not closed, but it is very crowded at the bottom, and a channel's fate in it shows up within the first handful of uploads. I ran 144 US Innertube searches (Shorts filter) and found 2,335 Shorts from 2,004 channels. I then pulled the full Shorts lists of 718 channels (136,602 Shorts) and exact dates via the Data API (about 600 units). Of the 500 new (created 2025+) English history-Shorts channels I found, 51 (10.2%) have hit 1M at least once. In the narrower story format (story niche plus Zack-type 3D), 14 of 177 have (7.9%). The other 85% never reached 100K, and the median channel's best Short is 1,700 views. The ATLAS cohort (created Aug–Oct 2026) has 248 channels with a median best of 1,200; 12 reached 100K and only 2 reached 1M. One of those two is PolySoldier: low-poly 3D nuclear and war oddities, 4.1M after 9 days and median 330K per Short. Winners break out fast: first 1M at median upload #10–12, about 2 weeks after the first Short. 27 of 32 channels with a 100K+ Short among their first 6 later hit 1M. Channels whose first 6 all stayed under 5K, which is ATLAS APE today (best 2,312), almost never get there: 0/42 by upload 50 in story format and 2/116 in broader history. My estimate, which is a hypothesis built on biased samples: continuing the current execution gives about a 1–3% chance of a first 1M within the next ~50 uploads. Rebuilding into a breakout format (mostly 3D animation, story-led, face-free) and treating it as a fresh launch gives roughly 5–10% by upload 30 and 8–12% by upload 50. Established players show mild fatigue (36 of 47 below their level of 12 months ago, median ratio 0.66), but the top still pulls millions: Zack D. Films' last-20 median is 13.5M, and it is now telling the same prison-escape and heist stories. All shares are upper bounds. Search discovery favours visible channels, and ATLAS APE itself appeared in none of the 2,335 results.

summary:
The core niche (absurd/weird true history in English) is crowded on supply but NOT saturated at the top.

- **Supply:** at least 138 channels uploaded a matching Short in the last 48 h, and 83 % of fresh uploads come from channels under 10K subscribers.
- **Ceiling:** 24 English core Shorts passed 1M views in the last 90 days, 7 of them from channels under a year old. The 2026 Data API top 50 for "weird history" holds 47 Shorts at ≥1M, against 43 in 2024.

The real obstacle is the newcomer base rate. A panel of 40 random active uploaders (picked because they uploaded, not because they were popular) gets a median of about 630 views per Short. 1.9 % of uploads reach ≥100K and 0.52 % reach ≥1M, which is roughly 1 in 190. Most of those 1M hits are 7–11 s clips, not 30–70 s narrated stories like ours.

ATLAS APE sits at the 68th percentile of that panel: an above-average newcomer, not a breakout.

Breakout newcomers own one repeatable series promise. FGtheexplainer runs "10 Weird Things You Didn't Know About X" at a median of 1.0M per Short, and World Ji Ke's country lists reach 1.6M. Channels that had one 1M hit on mixed topics fall back to medians of 2–10K. Copying a title template alone flops: copycats get a median of 1,570 views.

ATLAS APE has no such signature yet. Atlas's screen-time fell from 31 % to 0 % across the 6 uploads, the 6 Shorts use 5+ visual styles, and the banner promises geography.

What-if history maps give newcomers 9× more ≥100K hits per upload than the core niche (17 % vs 1.9 %), but fewer 1M slots. Mystery/unsolved is dead for newcomers.

The owner's German channel runs at the 95th–97th percentile of a German market whose newcomer baseline (median 1,175) matches the English one. Its edge is format and execution, not an easier market. German, however, has almost no 1M ceiling: 1 hit in 90 days in our sample.

Verdict: 1M is possible in English, but not by adding topics to the current mixed format. The channel needs one series format, one visual system and a fixed role for Atlas. The best-evidenced candidate is the proven Was Wäre Wenn map-question execution, ported to English.

Caveats:
- The panels are only 29–37 channels per niche.
- Subscriber counts are taken now, after any hit.
- Search keyword matching is loose.
- The 2025 change in Shorts view counting inflates 2026 numbers.

This analyst used 4,118 Data API units, including 27 search.list calls.

findings.claim: The newcomer base rate in the core niche is brutal, and ATLAS APE sits inside the crowd: an above-average newcomer, not a breakout. At the panel rate, a 1M hit takes about 190 uploads, and the 1M hits that do appear in this niche are mostly 7–11 s clips, not narrated stories.
findings.evidence: Uploader panel (40 random channels that uploaded in the last 48 h, their own Shorts aged 3–30 d): median 632 views, channel median 471. Per upload in the last 90 d: ≥10K 15.4 %, ≥100K 1.9 %, ≥1M 0.52 % (5 of 955 uploads, 4 channels) (raw/hit_rates.json). Our 3 Shorts aged 3–5 d (663 / 1,154 / 2,312) sit at the 51st / 65th / 76th percentiles; our channel median sits at the 68th percentile (raw/own_vs_panel.json). P(≥1 hit at 1M) = 27 % in 60 uploads, 41 % in 100. 3 of the 4 core panel 1M hits are 7–11 s clips (History Snap92 7 s, VortexX 8 s, ARCHIV 11 s). The median length of panel ≥100K hits is 11 s vs 46 s for all panel Shorts.
findings.action: Do not expect 1M from volume with the current narrated-story format. Its odds are likely below the 0.52 % average (hypothesis, N=5 hits). Execution must reach the top decile, where channel medians are ≥10K.

findings.claim: Among the adjacent niches, what-if history maps give newcomers the fattest middle tail: 9× more ≥100K hits per upload than the core niche. Its 1M ceiling is thinner. Mystery/unsolved is dead for newcomers.
findings.evidence: Per-upload rates for ≥10K / ≥100K / ≥1M (raw/hit_rates.json): what-if 35.9 % / 17.1 % / 0.99 %; core 15.4 % / 1.9 % / 0.52 %; science 24.0 % / 7.5 % / 1.03 %; animals 22.1 % / 6.1 % / 1.73 %; geo 18.9 % / 5.1 % / 0.52 %; survival 28.5 % / 6.0 % / 0.28 %; true crime 8.8 % / 2.8 % / 1.29 % (12 hits from 2 channels); mystery 1.2 % / 0.16 % / 0. Brand-new what-if channels: What If Bro (16 d, 1,070 subs) has 561K; Loco Brain Maps (15 d, 1,490 subs) has 425K. 90-d ≥1M found: what-if 11 vs core 24. The median length of what-if ≥100K hits is 14 s.
findings.action: For a fast floor of 10K–100K per Short, map what-if/why formats have the best measured newcomer odds. For 1M itself, core and animals/science have more slots. Avoid mystery/unsolved.

findings.claim: From 2024 to 2026 the 10M mega-tail thinned in fact niches, but the 1M tier held or grew in core, survival, animals and Spanish stories. The ceiling still exists.
findings.evidence: Data API search.list, same query, Jan 1–Oct 25 of each year, top 50 (raw/dapi_search.json, results.json year_compare). Count ≥1M, 2024 → 2026: core 43 → 47, survival 44 → 47, animals 48 → 48, es 42 → 48, what-if 17 → 23, mystery 8 → 16, geo 50 → 38, science 50 → 30, true crime 40 → 28. Count ≥10M: core 18 → 10, geo 25 → 3, science 24 → 5. Top-10 median: geo 31.1M → 6.9M, science 43.8M → 10.9M. 72 of 185 core all-time-popular results were published in 2026.
findings.action: Treat 1M per Short as realistic in core English and 10M+ as rare. Caveats: 2024 videos had 12 extra months to collect views, and the view-count change of 31.03.2025 inflates 2026 numbers. Both make the decline conservative, not exaggerated.

findings.claim: Breakout newcomers own one repeatable series promise: title shape, look and role. Channels that got one 1M hit with mixed topics fall back to a median of 2K–10K. One hit is luck; a series is a system.
findings.evidence: raw/breakouts_summary.json (yt-dlp metadata). FGtheexplainer (285 d): 48/109 titles «10 Weird Things You Didn't Know About [person]», median 1.0M, 50 % ≥1M. Why Guy (299 d), same template: median 1.1M, 57 % ≥1M. World Ji Ke (168 d), country-shape lists: median 1.6M, 71 % ≥1M. Meridian Anatomy (58 d), «X in 1000 years» maps: median 272K. Mixed-topic channels with one 1M hit: History Explorer (210 d), newest-20 median 1,850; GeoGlobeFiles (142 d), 5,300; Helivox (65 d), 2,800; Nikhil Panwar (196 d), 18,500. Survivorship bias: all 28 were selected because they had a 1M hit.
findings.action: Give the channel one series promise that is recognisable in 1 s (fixed title shape, visual system and host role) before adding topics.

findings.claim: Copying a winning template alone does not win. A copied title formula flops; a copied visual/sound gimmick does better. What is on screen carries the promise.
findings.evidence: raw/copycats.json (last 30 d, originator excluded). «10 weird things you didn't know about» copycats: 16 uploads by 12 channels, median 1,570 views, 6 % ≥100K (the originator's median is 1.0M). «Countries that look the same»: 41 uploads, median 7,034, 17 % ≥100K. «If history had sound»: 61 uploads, median 25,224, 31 % ≥100K. This agrees with the 23.10 finding that the same words do not give the same result.
findings.action: Define the series by its on-screen event per second and its frame 0, not only by the title wording. Check every cut with measure.py against the viral medians.

findings.claim: ATLAS APE has no recognisable signature. The orangutan is not used as a differentiator: he is an intro/outro host whose screen-time shrank to zero. Every Short uses a different visual language, and the banner promises another channel.
findings.evidence: sheets/*_1fps.jpg, raw/own_atlas_screen_census.json. Atlas share of seconds: Volcano 16/77 = 21 %, Rabbits 19/63 = 31 %, Yellow Fleet 6/33 = 19 %, Pig War 4/42 = 10 %, farm girl 2/33 = 6 % (tiny icon), Russell 0/44 = 0 %. In frame 0 only in the first two. 5+ visual systems in 6 Shorts (DEM + toy 3D, low-poly 3D, toy-3D ships, AI-photoreal + flat vector, AI Pixar-like, flat vector). Banner «GEOGRAPHY · MAPS · FACTS», description empty, 4 subs from 5,239 views (data/2026-10-25/channel.json, summary.json). N=6 shows no relation between Atlas screen-time and views (Yellow Fleet 2,312 views with 19 %; Russell 1,174 at 10 h with 0 %).
findings.action: Decide once. Either Atlas becomes the recurring protagonist of the series (in the first 2 s, the same role every time) or he stays as the avatar only. Lock one visual system, and fix the banner and description to the real promise.

findings.claim: The owner's German channel shows his execution beats the market base rate by a wide margin. It does so in a fixed-promise format (one question per Short on an animated map), not in a softer market: the German newcomer baseline matches the English one.
findings.evidence: Was Wäre Wenn, October 2026: 29 Shorts, median 87,587, min 17,653, max 511,363, 13 ≥100K, 0 ≥1M, total 4.22M (raw/wwW_shorts_dapi.json). German panel median Short = 1,175 vs English core 632 and what-if 944 (results.json panel). WWW's median Short sits at the 95th percentile of German panel uploads; its channel median at the 97th (raw/own_vs_panel.json). Its worst October Short (17.6K) is 7.6× the best ATLAS Short (2.3K). Its October Shorts are 60–74 s long.
findings.action: Port the proven WWW execution (one question per Short on an animated map, fixed title shape, one look) into English as the ATLAS series, or as a parallel A/B series. Language and format are confounded (N=1 channel), so test before betting the channel on it.

findings.claim: German has a high floor but almost no 1M ceiling for history Shorts. English has a lower floor for us but many more 1M slots. For the stated 1M goal, English is the right market.
findings.evidence: German-language history Shorts ≥1M in 90 d (Innertube popularity buckets, 4 keywords): 1, max 1.63M. English core with the same method: 9; with the Data API added: 24 (raw/innertube_ceiling_90d.json, results.json). German panel ≥1M per upload: 0.49 % (4 uploads, 3 channels, partly off-topic). WWW's maximum after 37 Shorts is 511K.
findings.action: Keep German for reliable reach. Aim for 1M in English, using the format that already works in German.

findings.claim: Search-based samples of «fresh uploads» over-represent winners by 7–131×. Earlier search-based conclusions (e.g. «fresh uploads get 1–2K») need this correction.
findings.evidence: Search-sample median at 3–30 d vs panel median: core 10,576 vs 632 (×17), what-if 45,286 vs 944 (×48), survival ×38, true crime ×47, mystery ×131, es ×7, de ×9 (results.json). Panel N = 29–37 channels with qualifying Shorts per niche; subscriber counts are taken now, after any hit.
findings.action: Use scripts/panel.py + scripts/hit_rates.py (about 80 Data API units per niche) as the baseline for future niche and format decisions; do not use search-ranked samples.

The per-upload 1M rate (5 of 955) is not a lottery that volume can win. All 5 hits came from the 4 channels whose own median is 16.6K–41K. 0 of the 805 uploads from channels with a median under 10K reached 1M, and only 3 reached 100K.

verdicts.corrected_claim:
The search.list numbers reproduce:
- Core ≥10M: 18 → 10.
- Core top-10 median: 24.3M → 16.7M.
- Geo and science mega-tails fell sharply.

The interpretation does not hold, for three reasons:
- '≥1M in a top-50 ranked by views' is a capped metric. Core is 93 % vs 94 %, the same share, so it shows the 1M tier held, not that it grew.
- The two biases point in opposite directions. The 2024 videos' extra 12 months of views exaggerates the decline; the 2025 view-count change hides it. The analyst wrongly said both make the decline conservative.
- Loose keyword matching adds off-topic and non-English videos in both years.

A defensible reading: 1M-level Shorts still appear every year, and the 10M+ tail is thinner, by an amount that cannot be quantified from this data.

verdicts.corrected_claim:
Was Wäre Wenn's October Shorts are at the 95th percentile of German panel uploads, and its channel median at the 97th. That is far above the market, so the edge is mostly execution and format.
- N=29, median 87,587, minimum 17,653 (at about 21 h old), maximum 511,363, 13 Shorts ≥100K, total 4.22M, lengths 60–74 s.
- But the German newcomer baseline does not match the English one. The German panel median is 1,175 vs 632 for English core (×1.9), the channel median is ×2.5, and the ≥100K rate per upload is 8.0 % vs 1.9 % (×4.2). German is a softer market for 100K.
- Was Wäre Wenn is not a newcomer: created 2025-08-26, 4,240 subs. Its own Aug–Sep Shorts had 3.6–5.7K views before the October format change (about a 15–24× jump within the same channel, N=1, confounded with topic and posting twice a day).
- English panel data do not support porting it: English what-if Shorts ≥45 s reach ≥100K at only 2.4 %, the same as core. Treat the port as an untested A/B test, not as the best-evidenced option.

But the uploader panel's per-upload ≥1M rate is equal: German 0.49 % (4 of 813) vs English core 0.52 % (5 of 955). All of these hits are off-topic (religious-death shock, police clips) on both sides, and German has a ×4 higher ≥100K rate. 'English has more 1M slots' is plausible but weakly evidenced. verdicts.corrected_claim: Search-ranked samples of fresh uploads overstate typical views by 7–131× vs the uploader panel; for core it is 10,576 vs 632 (×17). One caveat: the panel itself over-samples prolific uploaders. Its hit rates are dominated by 1–3 channels per niche, so they should be read per channel tier, not as niche-wide lotteries.
verdicts.note: Recomputed results.json niches.*.views_age_3_30d.median against panel.*.median for all 10 niches, and all factors match. The channel concentration is in verify/panel_recut.json: top-3 channels hold 13 of 18 core, 89 of 121 what-if and 45 of 65 German ≥100K hits.

missed: Hits are a property of channels, not of niches. In every niche, the top 3 channels hold 72–100 % of the ≥100K hits. Channels with a median under 10K reach ≥100K at 0–1.4 % per upload, and 0 of 805 core uploads from such channels hit 1M (verify/panel_recut.json). So niche choice is second-order: the decisive task is raising the channel median ×10 through execution.

The closest successful format to ATLAS already dominates the core niche: narrated 40–70 s 'weird history/animals' Shorts with mixed topics (Hoodie Guy, Why Guy, FGtheexplainer). Their first uploads were already at 92K–24M (lifetime views, inflated by later growth), so the gap to us looks like an execution gap of 100× or more. The analyst never measured their execution: frame 0, motion, presenter and VO pace. That is what the owner explicitly asks for (analyze execution, not topics). Doing it needs owner approval to download a few reference Shorts.

Long narrated Shorts on new channels do reach 1M in 2026, against the '1M hits are 7–11 s clips' claim. Jim's Wormhole (21 days old) has 161–172 s Shorts at 2.9M and 2.7M. Map Warden (132 days old) has 'The Falklands: A 300-Year Fight', 94 s, 5.9M (verify/ceiling_story_queries_d90.json), which is a Pig-War-type territorial absurdity.

Audience geography was ignored. ATLAS Analytics views come 35.5 % from the US, 22.4 % from PH, 7.7 % from IN, 6.7 % from ID and 5.0 % from MY; Anglo countries total about 46 % and South/Southeast Asia about 45 %. PH has the lowest average view % at 48. The newcomer what-if 'proof' channels win with India and Southeast Asia country-pride titles. Whose country a story is about is both a lever and a confound for any 'English market' comparison.

The owner's own interest signals are absent from the saturation verdict. Shares are 0 on all 4 Analytics-covered Shorts, and the channel has 4 subscribers from 5,239 views (summary.json, channel.json). For 'is the audience interested?' these matter more than percentile rank among mass uploaders.

The '68th percentile, above-average newcomer' framing flatters ATLAS. The panel is size-biased toward prolific, often mass-produced channels, and many have medians under 100. The meaningful bar is the top-decile core channel median of about 16.6K, which ATLAS (1,154) misses by about ×14.

Was Wäre Wenn's strongest evidence is within one channel and was not used. Its Aug–Sep 2026 Shorts got 5,745 and 3,640 views. After switching to 60–74 s what-if/why map Shorts at about 2 per day, the October median was 87.6K. A same-channel jump of about 15–24× after a format change is direct evidence for 'execution/format beats niche' (N=1, confounded with topic, frequency and channel history).

The analyst's own data contradict its action items. The recommended WWW port has no English support: what-if ≥45 s reaches ≥100K at 2.4 %, the same as core. The 'series title first' action is contradicted by the analyst's own title-stem data and by FGtheexplainer's history. The 'avoid mystery' action is contradicted by Jim's Wormhole in the analyst's own core panel.
